tcp_p2_s: The other one shows up when you get close to something painful, as a sudden pull to do anything but feel it (even a yawn can come with an "I'm so done with this" feeling). It might believe there's no grown-up around who could hold what's coming up. I'd want out too. That yawn might actually be the opposite, though. Re-evaluation Counseling, a kind of peer counseling, counts yawning as emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out. The skeptic and the pull both started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and they can keep at it even when what they do now hurts you. If you treat either one like an enemy, or like proof that something's wrong with you, it'll probably just think "See? I knew it," and stay in charge. I wonder what it would do if it didn't have to.

wcs_p1_ready: Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I'd want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never had to find out. Before either one, I'd look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes those weeks were mostly reading about it and getting ready, which can feel a lot like doing it (this article included). Or you did sit down with your little one, and fear got there first, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. It can be as plain as never having the place to yourself. Whatever it turns out to be, I'd work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything.
wcs_p2_joel: Maybe you've been trying to comfort your little one for weeks, and the words are all there, but the loving grown-up behind them isn't, not yet. Some people at that point might try saying sweeter and sweeter things, and then upon that not working, perhaps just "throw the baby out with the bathwater," and decide reparenting is useless. I'd borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.
wcs_p5_w1: Sometimes it's the exercise that works. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you're skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people's first guess is that they didn't go deep enough. I don't think that's it, though, and I don't think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn't come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I'd try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. It doesn't have to happen after every session, and once isn't proof you've got it all down.
